newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - LME seen quiet on U.S. holiday.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - LME seen quiet on U.S. holiday.

text.p: Base metal prices in the London Metal Exchange (LME) may take a breather and drift lower on Friday because of the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, metal traders said.
"It should be quiet and thin because of the U.S. holiday," the general manager for a European metal trading company said, adding three month copper prices may come down to around US$2,240 a tonne.

"When it's thin and quiet, the tendency is for prices to come down. Copper should slide slowly. $2,200 a tonne is the floor. That's the main support for the day," a dealer for a Singapore-based metal firm said.
Three month copper closed the afternoon kerb in London on Thursday at $2,255 a tonne, down from six month highs of $2,313 a tonne.
Copper was priced at around $2,255/60 a tonne by Singapore metal dealers at 0300 GMT.
"It's impossible to pick where copper is going. It's been incredibly volatile," a senior dealer said.
"Copper may well be headed to its pre-Hamanaka level of $2,600 a tonne," the managing director of a Japanese metal trading company said.
He was refering to the level of copper prices before the dismissal of star copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, whose $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper losses led to his firing by Sumitomo Corp last June.
Prices nosedived in the wake of the scandal and hit lows of just under $1,800 a tonne in the LME.
Traders here were also paying closer attention to the amount of copper moving into Singapore warehouses.
"About 10,000 tonnes has arrived in the past week," a dealer said, adding he expected another 5,000 tonnes to arrive next week.
"Most of the material was re-exported by China and they're banking on making a $200 a tonne profit on it," a Japanese trader said. "They'll probably buy it back later when prices come off."
A majority of Singapore-based dealers expect copper stocks to rise for the first time in more than 10 weeks by about 2,000 to 6,000 tonnes.

But one dealer said that while copper is expected to rise by up to 6,000 tonnes, he would not be surprised if stocks fell by 20,000 tonnes because of uncertainty regarding the amount of material moving to warehouses.
"The uncertainty is about how much material is going to the LME. That's why there's such a stock variation of 6,000 tonnes up and 20,000 tonnes down," the dealer said.

Only a fraction of the material has been placed on warrant in Singapore. The amount of copper in the LME's Singapore warehouse reached 7,925 tonnes on Tuesday, down 700 tonnes from last Friday's level.
On the other hand, aluminium stocks will probably slide by around 3,000-4,000 tonnes when the LME report is released at 0900 GMT, traders said.

"Aluminium prices should come off a little because of the U.S. holiday," an aluminium dealer for a Japanese commodity house said. "But aluminium is well supported. If the (three month) price breaks through $1,570, it will go to over $1,600 a tonne."
Aluminium prices were quoted in Singapore at around $1,552/57 a tonne at 0300 GMT compared with the kerb close in London on Thursday of $1,555 a tonne, dealers said.
Base metal premiums in the city-state eased across the board on slow demand for some and ample stocks for others, traders said.
